cards.title: Calculate CAC and LTGP monthly as your two core operating metrics
cards.summary: Every DTC brand should compute cost to acquire a customer and constrained lifetime gross profit each month, then treat them as the fundamental diagnostic instead of ROAS.
cards.use_when: You need a single monthly scorecard to decide whether the store can profitably scale paid acquisition, cut spend, or fix retention.
steps: Compute CAC = total ad spend across all platforms in the period divided by new customers acquired in that same period. Pull new customers from your own order data, not from a platform summary.
Compute LTGP = gross profit from a customer over a fixed window, where gross profit means revenue minus cost of goods AND cost of delivery (shipping/fulfilment), not just revenue minus COGS.

Choose the window based on how often your category repeats: use first-purchase gross profit (a very short window) for repurchase-poor categories like furniture and homewares; extend to roughly 180 or 365 days for consumables, supplements and subscription models.

Pull the lifetime figure from a real cohort analysis (cohorts of customers by acquisition month, tracked forward to day 30/60/90/etc.), not from attributed revenue dashboards, daily returning-customer revenue, or a 'percent new customers' Shopify tile.

Record both numbers every month in one table so you can see the trend. When either CAC rises or LTGP falls, drill into that metric first rather than assuming it is a creative, seasonality or traffic problem.

Timestamp every structural change (new product, new channel, new agency, heavier discounting) and read it against the CAC and LTGP series to see whether the change improved the ratio, then double down or reverse.
caveats: Applying an assumed gross-margin percentage to cohort revenue is a workaround; the source says generating it from actual cost of goods is better.
Platform-attributed ROAS can stay stable while the real business declines, because view-through and over-crediting inflate it.
cards.source_name: The Death Spiral That Kills Most eCommerce Brands.docx

cards.title: Read the LTGP:CAC bands and know what each one demands
cards.summary: LTGP:CAC below 1 is a death spiral, 1-2 needs extremely lean opex, 2-3 is the source's target scaling zone, and above 3 suggests underinvesting in acquisition.
cards.use_when: You are setting a paid-media budget or deciding whether to push spend harder, hold, or pull back on acquisition.
steps: Diagnose your current position: if LTGP is $100 and CAC is $120, the ratio is below 1 and you lose $20 on the first purchase. The source treats sub-1 as structurally dangerous unless retention is genuinely exceptional, which it calls very rare.

Recognise the 1-2 band as workable but tight: at $1 in and $1.50 out in gross profit, the 50 cents must cover operating expenses, so you need unusually lean opex or very large volume to produce a healthy net margin. The source says it is possible to run here with strong operations and retention, just uncommon.
Treat 2-3 as the zone where the source always suggests scaling and ramping budgets.
Treat above 3 as a signal you are leaving money on the table and should ramp harder.

Do not chase a fantasy ratio: LTGP is bounded by category structure. A low-ticket product (e.g. a $50 supplement) cannot deliver an arbitrary multiple, so benchmark against the best operators in your own category and set a realistic CAC target from there.
caveats: These bands are the presenter's heuristics for DTC ecommerce, not a universal law, and they assume ecommerce dynamics (weak consumer stickiness) rather than service or B2B models.
The bands assume LTGP is measured over the correct window for your repurchase frequency; comparing a 30-day LTGP to a 365-day CAC benchmark is meaningless.
cards.source_name: The Death Spiral That Kills Most eCommerce Brands.docx

cards.title: Derive CAC from CPM, CTR and conversion rate to offset rising ad costs
cards.summary: CAC = CPC / conversion rate, and CPC = CTR x CPM, so annually rising CPMs can be offset by lifting click-through rate or conversion rate.
cards.use_when: Your CAC is climbing and you need to decide which lever — ad creative, PDP/landing page conversion, or media efficiency — to work on.
steps: Write out the chain: CAC = CPC / conversion rate and CPC = CTR x CPM, so CPM sits several layers beneath CAC via CPC.
Accept the structural premise the source states: platforms need to grow revenue every year, so CPMs will very likely be higher next year. Plan for it rather than treating it as a crisis.
Offset that lift by improving either CTR or conversion rate. If you lift one of them enough, you hold your profitability roughly flat year over year even as CPMs rise.

For ecommerce application: CTR improvements come from creative and offer framing in the ad, while conversion-rate improvements come from the PDP, landing page, offer clarity, pricing presentation and checkout. Assign the fix to the right surface rather than defaulting to 'creative'.

Set a discipline of compounding small improvements — the source frames it as improving about 1% a day on CTR and conversion. Operators who stay better than the majority keep feeling less CPM pressure and can push budget harder when competitors pull back.
Note that platform algorithm updates are designed to lift advertiser ROI so the platform can then raise CPMs; the platform does not hand you the surplus, so your own improvement is the offset.
caveats: This is a decomposition, not a prediction; conversion rate here means purchase conversion on your traffic, not lead conversion.
CTR and CPM interact with audience and placement; a CTR gain on cheap placements may not translate into cheaper CAC.
cards.source_name: The Death Spiral That Kills Most eCommerce Brands.docx

cards.title: Split the P&L into first-time and returning customer views
cards.summary: Filter every P&L line by order-type tag to expose an acquisition loss that a combined, blended P&L hides behind returning-customer profit.
cards.use_when: Total profit still looks acceptable but you suspect new-customer acquisition has quietly turned loss-making, or before raising capital or debt.
steps: Tag orders in your commerce platform by first-time versus returning customer, then generate two full P&Ls by filtering every line item on that tag.

Read total profit contribution at the bottom of each. A brand can lose, illustratively, $50,000 a month on the first-time-customer P&L while making $300,000 on the returning-customer P&L, so the business looks profitable while acquisition is bleeding.
Track the trend in the first-time P&L specifically: the source's example is a client falling from +$20,000/month on first-time customers to -$70,000/month, invisible in the blended view.

Use this split when deciding whether returning revenue is genuinely subsidising acquisition or merely masking it. If returning profit is not covering the first-time loss, the model is fragile and any retention wobble becomes an existential event.
If a full split is impractical, use the unit-level LTGP:CAC ratio as the everyday proxy — the source says it tells you the same story at unit level that the P&L split tells you at volume level.

Pair the split with a cohort view of CAC month over month and new-customer volume month over month, since the pattern the source describes is CAC exploding and spend being cranked up to hold volume, after which CAC never recovers.
caveats: Requires reliable order-type tagging; mis-tagged orders corrupt both P&Ls.
The dollar figures cited are illustrative case examples from the presenter's audits, not benchmarks for your store.
cards.source_name: The Death Spiral That Kills Most eCommerce Brands.docx

cards.title: Diagnose the death spiral from the two numbers, not from traffic, creative or seasonality
cards.summary: The spiralling CAC pattern — CAC rises, new customers fall, spend is increased to hold revenue, CAC rises again — is structural and should be diagnosed from the CAC and LTGP series first.
cards.use_when: Revenue or profitability has deteriorated for a quarter and leadership is blaming traffic, creative fatigue, seasonality or the macroeconomy.
steps: Trace the described loop: CAC creeps from, say, $50 to $60; at a fixed $100,000 budget you acquire fewer customers; revenue falls; with weak repeat purchasing you increase spend to hold revenue; the extra spend pushes CAC higher again, and it can end up double the prior level.

Before accepting any other explanation, pull CAC month over month alongside new-customer volume and revenue month over month. The signature is CAC breaking upward and spend being cranked up afterwards to maintain volume.

Reject the three default misdiagnoses the source names — that it is a traffic problem (just needs more spend or cheaper CPCs), a creative problem (creative drives targeting so it must be the ads), or a seasonality/macro problem. In the source's experience across 1,000+ audits, it is usually none of these.
Work backwards from LTGP and CAC to identify the actual constraint, then fix that constraint rather than adding spend on top of a broken unit economic.
Be aware that forcing scale through a bad LTGP with raised capital does not work; the source states that the ratio, not the funding, determines whether the business can scale.
caveats: The source acknowledges operating expenses can also sink brands, particularly smaller ones ($50k-$300k/month), often causing cash-constrained failure rather than a pure LTGP:CAC failure.
The audit volume and client scale cited are the presenter's own experience, not an independent study.
cards.source_name: The Death Spiral That Kills Most eCommerce Brands.docx

cards.title: Rank your measurement methods by distance from base reality
cards.summary: Move up a hierarchy from expert opinion and platform ROAS to multi-regression, quasi-experiments and geo holdouts, because decisions are only as good as how closely the metric tracks reality.
cards.use_when: You need to decide how much to trust a platform-reported number before reallocating budget between channels or scaling spend.
steps: Place methods on the ladder: expert opinion plus anecdote at the bottom, then simple correlation (platform-attributed ROAS), then advanced correlation such as multi-regression or marketing mix modelling, then quasi-experiments such as difference-in-differences or regression discontinuity, then true experiments such as geo holdouts at the top.

Prefer the highest rung you can practically run for the decision at hand; the source's framing is that the highest-ROI activity in business is making the correct decision, which requires seeing reality as clearly as possible.

Sanity-check platform numbers by removing view-through conversions first. In the source's example, a reported ROAS that looked like ~20 collapsed to ~7 once view-throughs were stripped out, and dropped again when narrowed to a stricter attribution model.
Watch the de-inflated number over time rather than the topline: a de-inflated figure declining month over month is the early warning the topline hides.

Where you spend across multiple platforms, use experimental design (holdouts, quasi-experiments) to attribute contribution, because LTGP:CAC alone cannot tell you which platform drove the good or bad result.
Keep LTGP:CAC as the ultimate scorecard of business health even while using experiments to explain why it moved.
caveats: The source explicitly says avoiding all of this by simply watching LTGP:CAC is acceptable for many operators — the hierarchy is for platform-level attribution decisions.
The specific ROAS collapse figures are a single anonymised client example.
cards.source_name: The Death Spiral That Kills Most eCommerce Brands.docx

cards.title: Match your CAC discipline to the retention structure of your category
cards.summary: Furniture and homewares should run on first-purchase gross profit with a deliberately flat CAC, while fashion and CPG can extend the LTGP window because repeat revenue genuinely accrues.
cards.use_when: You are setting the measurement window and CAC target for your category, or deciding whether to invest in retention or defend acquisition cost.
steps: Classify your category's repeat behaviour. The source cites day-365 gross-profit lift benchmarks of about 55% for fashion, about 110% for CPG and supplements, and near 0% for furniture and homewares.

For repurchase-poor categories (furniture, homewares), treat lifetime gross profit as effectively nonexistent and manage the business on first-purchase gross profit with a stable CAC. The source's operational guidance for these clients is to keep CAC flat over time.

For categories with genuine repeat behaviour (fashion, CPG, supplements, subscription), extend the LTGP window out to around 180-365 days and use cohort data to measure it, while still keeping CAC controlled.

Do not assume retention tactics can transform a low-lift category. The source argues the achievable LTGP band is largely structurally predetermined by industry and price point, and that executing many retention tactics will not move a number that the business model fixes.
Pick CAC benchmarks from the best operators in your specific industry rather than from cross-industry ratios, then aim to approach them.

Recognise the source's own estimate that roughly 80% of brands have weak lifetime gross profit contribution (often only 20-40% gross-profit lift by day 365), in which case CAC control is the primary lever.
caveats: The 55% / 110% / near-0% figures are the presenter's cited vertical benchmarks, not a universal measurement standard.
B2B has materially different repeat dynamics from D2C and is called out as a different game.
cards.source_name: The Death Spiral That Kills Most eCommerce Brands.docx

cards.title: Use cohort analysis to read retention instead of surface retention metrics
cards.summary: Shopify-style cohort boxes, read forward in time, are the source's required method for measuring lifetime gross profit and retention rather than Klaviyo attributed revenue or daily returning-customer revenue.
cards.use_when: You want to measure retention properly to set your LTGP window and confirm whether recent acquisition cohorts are degrading.
steps: Open cohort analysis and read month zero as revenue from a customer on day one, then follow the same cohort forward to day 30, 60, 90 and beyond to see its cumulative value.

Reject the metrics the source explicitly disqualifies for this purpose: Klaviyo attributed revenue, returning-customer revenue measured daily or monthly, and the percentage-of-new-customers tile in Shopify.
Pull the column matching your chosen window (for example the day-90 column) and convert that revenue to gross profit using actual cost of goods where possible.
Compare that LTGP figure to the CAC recorded in the acquisition month for the same cohort to produce a windowed LTGP:CAC ratio per cohort.

Look across cohorts, not just in aggregate: the source's example is November cohorts being markedly worse than adjacent months because of product portfolio changes and margin compression from discounting, which drags the extended lifetime window down.

Use the cohort view to spot margin compression: even when CAC is stable month to month, first-purchase gross profit can swing from, illustratively, $70 to $40 depending on discounting and portfolio mix.
caveats: Native cohort reporting may not display gross profit, so the source builds a custom cohort analysis to get GP rather than revenue.
The illustrative $70/$40 and November-cohort examples are from anonymised client audits, not general benchmarks.
cards.source_name: The Death Spiral That Kills Most eCommerce Brands.docx

cards.title: Three legitimate ways to fund a sub-1 LTGP:CAC — and who should not use them
cards.summary: Losses on first purchase can be funded by returning-customer profit, investor capital, or debt, but the source warns that capital- and debt-funded models demand an advanced operator.
cards.use_when: You are deliberately losing money on first purchase and must choose how the gap gets financed, or you are evaluating whether to take investment or debt to scale acquisition.
steps: Option one: fund it with repeat purchase. If returning-customer profit contribution reliably exceeds the first-time-customer loss, the business is profitable overall even while acquisition loses money. Verify with the two-P&L split rather than assuming.
Option two: raise capital. The source does not call this inherently bad and notes that many fast-scaling DTC brands used capital to drive content network effects and aggressive ad scaling.
Option three: use creditors/debt. The source's caution is that debt makes profitability visibility more complex, so it requires a dialled-in operator.

Screen yourself against the source's stated threshold: it would not work with a $6-7m revenue brand carrying investors or creditors, calling the risk profile enormous and saying it has rarely seen them do well. This is an opinion, not a rule.
Regardless of funding source, keep measuring LTGP:CAC monthly so the funding decision is based on the real acquisition economics rather than a blended P&L that looks fine.
caveats: The source's position on not serving $6-7m brands with investors or creditors is that presenter's own risk preference and agency policy, not a universal law.
None of these options fixes a structurally negative ratio; they only buy time to fix it.
cards.source_name: The Death Spiral That Kills Most eCommerce Brands.docx

cards.title: Treat operating-expense creep as a separate cash-risk failure mode from the death spiral
cards.summary: Smaller brands can fail from over-invested operating expenses that compress margin, force debt for inventory, and end in a cash constraint rather than a ratio problem.
cards.use_when: You are setting opex and hiring plans for a smaller store (roughly $50k-$300k/month) and must protect working capital for inventory.
steps: Track whether margin is being compressed by opex growth, not just by CAC or COGS. The source's diagnosis of many small brands is that they overinvested in operating expenses while being poor capital allocators.

Model the downstream effect: compressed margin leaves less cash, which pushes you to take debt to purchase future inventory, which pressures the whole financial position and can end in failure from a cash constraint rather than a bad LTGP:CAC.
Before adding fixed cost, confirm your current LTGP:CAC can carry it. The source notes that a better ratio would have paid for the opex in these cases, so the ratio is still the root fix.
If your store sits in the low band of LTGP:CAC (1-2), apply extra scrutiny to every fixed-cost addition, because that band requires unusually lean operating expenses to produce acceptable net profit.
Distinguish this failure mode explicitly from the acquisition death spiral when diagnosing a declining store, so you apply the right corrective action.
caveats: This observation is drawn from the presenter's early-agency experience with roughly 300-400 SMB ecommerce brands over three years, not a controlled study.
The $50k-$300k/month band is the source's observed range for this pattern, not a hard threshold.
cards.source_name: The Death Spiral That Kills Most eCommerce Brands.docx

cards.title: Treat first-purchase liquidity as the ecommerce norm, not the service-business norm
cards.summary: Unlike services where payback can stretch over months, consumer ecommerce brands should aim to be as profitable and liquid as possible on the first purchase because consumer stickiness is weak.
cards.use_when: You are setting payback expectations and acquisition targets, and deciding whether to accept a long first-purchase payback period.
steps: Stop importing service-business logic. The source notes agencies often break even around month 4-6 after acquisition costs because businesses repeat-transact for years; consumers are lucky to make a second purchase and rarer still a third.
Set the ecommerce default to near-breakeven or better on the first purchase, and treat anything materially below that as a risk position unless retention is genuinely exceptional.

If your LTGP:CAC is below 1, quantify the requirement precisely: applying an assumed percentage of cohort revenue to get gross profit and using an illustrative $100 LTGP against a $120 CAC gives a $20 first-purchase loss per customer.
If you must run a long payback, make it survivable with genuine measured repeat revenue rather than hoped-for retention — see the two-P&L split for verification.
Communicate the difference in expectation internally: this card is about purchase conversion and repeat purchasing, not sales close rate or lead conversion, which follow different payback logic.
caveats: The source's framing assumes D2C consumer behaviour; B2B and service models have different stickiness and payback tolerance.
The $100/$120 example is illustrative arithmetic, not an industry standard.
cards.source_name: The Death Spiral That Kills Most eCommerce Brands.docx

cards.title: Use owned channels for returning revenue while accepting that new acquisition is rented
cards.summary: Email, SMS, community and brand reduce dependence on paid traffic for repeat revenue, but the source argues new-customer acquisition almost always involves renting attention.
cards.use_when: You are allocating effort between paid acquisition and list/community ownership, or pushback arises that paid should be abandoned in favour of owned channels.
steps: Classify your demand sources: renting is paying for traffic that disappears when payment stops; owning is assets you keep, such as an email list, an SMS list, or a community.
Direct owned-channel effort primarily at the LTGP side of the equation, since the source says list and community value largely sits under returning-customer revenue and drives repeat purchase.

Accept that new-customer acquisition remains rented in most forms. The source's reasoning: you acquire a customer first and only then hold first-party data to remarket to, and even large organic followings do not guarantee delivery of a post to that audience.
Do not adopt the dogma that you should never pay for attention. Keep improving owned assets while continuing to rent space to bring in new customers, then convert them into owned relationships.
Note the source's defence of the 'own your list' rhetoric as correct but incomplete — it is a large and worthwhile focus on the retention side, not a replacement for paid acquisition.
caveats: The source is explicitly arguing against the position that rising CPMs mean paid is dead and email is the answer.
Organic reach limitations are illustrated by the presenter's own account (roughly 50,000 followers getting far fewer views per post) — an anecdote, not a platform-wide measurement.
cards.source_name: The Death Spiral That Kills Most eCommerce Brands.docx

cards.title: Timestamp and measure big structural changes against CAC and LTGP
cards.summary: Every major business change — new agency, new channel, new product launch, heavier ad volume — should be dated and then read back against the CAC and LTGP historical series to see if the ratio improved.
cards.use_when: You are deciding whether to repeat, roll back or expand an investment such as a product launch, a new ad platform, or a change in creative partner.
steps: Before making the change, record the current CAC and LTGP baseline and the date the change goes live.

After the change, compare the post-change values against the historical series. The source's example: a March product launch that raised LTGP — expected, because portfolio diversity increases cross-sell opportunity.
Ask explicitly whether the ratio improved, and then whether you can afford to repeat the action without putting the balance sheet at risk.
Double down and iterate in the direction of changes that demonstrably improved the ratio rather than judging them on gut feel or a single month's revenue.

Apply the same test to structural decisions such as introducing a new platform (e.g. Snapchat) or significantly increasing ad volume, since those consume capital and must earn their place on the ratio.

Avoid the failure pattern the source describes: a store whose monthly profit slid from, illustratively, $100,000 to $80,000 while nobody checked the first-time-customer P&L, which had swung from positive to deeply negative.
caveats: Requires sufficient data after each change to separate signal from normal variance; short windows may mislead.
The $100k/$80k and March-launch examples are from anonymised client work, not guaranteed outcomes.
